I—in Germany in 1953—know less about my own situation than the young Mexican whom the Mexican priests in the year 1500 first fed well and then slaughtered knew about his. So please spare me any more questioning and questionnaire-ing.
Meanwhile the Holy Father in Rome is interested neither in me nor in the brave Slovak Tiso, but in the unbaptized atomic spy Julius Rosenberg, and sends a telegram to Washington.
That is the religion of humanity.
Blank verse—to the tune of the Horst Wessel Song:
Do not fool yourself: the last Christian was Hegel; the last katechon. The axis was and remains the Son of God; Watch yourself—the Devil has already taken note. Yet with Christ at skittles.
Whenever things seem to be going especially well for me, I tell myself: I know no more about my situation than the young Mexican whom the priests first fed and then slaughtered knew about his.
“In Germany today, the intellectual worker has become an off-the-books worker.”
So says the Frankfurt Society for Economic Policy, founded in 1947, in the year 1952, p. …
What a genuine Worker, in Ernst Jünger’s sense!
Let us begin our new song:
Off-the-books work is my delight! At the earliest hour I descend Into the darkest tunnel far and wide. Greetings, Germany, from the very bottom!
“Situation ethics, compare p. 54 [= newspaper clipping p. 279].”
The problem of error in persona—mistaken identity—as grounds for invalidity.”

The invisible order is stronger and deeper than the visible one. Heraclitus says this, and in doing so strikes directly at the claim made by the visible Church. Yet this very same visible Church describes the power it claims as an indirect power, a potestas indirecta.
Original: visible and at the same time indirect.

Le secret de l’église catholique—c’est qu’il n’y a pas de pouvoir indirect. The secret of the Catholic Church is that there is no such thing as indirect power. Can this strange combination of visibility and indirectness still be held together by the old formula of a complexio oppositorum—a union of opposites?
You betrayed the wine—by taking the chalice away from the laity.
And now you are surprised that all of it, under the banner of Democracy, has you by the throat?
Luther, Hamann, Bruno Bauer turned your wine unbearably sour.

What, after all, is nihilism? When a human being travels at more than forty kilometres an hour, gentlemen: that is nihilism. A thoroughly un-Scholastic answer. A nihilistic answer—in the eyes of the frauds.
Jean Bodin’s advice: Never challenge the fury of the people.

What is law? (What is God? Today the two are the same.) Something that is valid, and that is successfully made valid—with a real chance of forcing obedience—which means something that can be enforced by coercion.
So what is a jurist? Someone whose profession is making things legally valid. A professional enforcer of validity. These validity-makers are worse than the money-makers.
From the positivist point of view—that is, when there is a clearly defined and predictable legal rule—things are still manageable.
But God help us when natural-law infiltration—begins, and broad general clauses start being enforced!
“The death of the ruler; newspapers from 5 March 1953.”
“March 1954, one year later: the seriously ill Holy Father is suffering from hiccups.
Summer 1954: he has Niehans’s fresh-cell treatment injected into him so that he can live a little longer.”
On the page to the left:
“On this, Khrushchev’s speech at the Twentieth Congress of the Communist Party of the Soviet Union, February 1956, and de-Stalinization in spring 1956!!
The revelation of the complete speech at the beginning of June 1956.
And the Pope’s death in 1958, with Galeazzi-Lisi.
Thanks to Niehans’s fresh cells, he lived long enough to witness de-Stalinization.
No doubt a miracle through God’s providence and <…>.”
But what am I? I am a survivor. I have neither been standardized into a professional validity-enforcer nor infiltrated by natural law. I am neither a full enforcer nor an empty one.
I have no insurance of any kind. I would regard it as an insult to the great universal insurer—the “welfare state”—if I were to permit myself any additional insurance.
But every status quo wants eternity and demands oaths of eternal loyalty.
By doing precisely that, it reduces the oath itself to mere legality.
Then—there finally arise, through terrible torture and persecution, the free oaths, the conjurations, and the new men who are once again capable of oath, of God, and of power.
“A sympathetic poem about women, in the manner of Gertrud von Le Fort and Claudel.”
Now I am old. Now I have crossed the age limit.
I must go away, and you, my darling, stay here.
“Here” means: on the other side of the age limit.
So now I am old. And whom do I meet on the far side of the line? Man and Democracy. Well, that truly is the opposite of paradise.
Absolute Man—not even enlightened absolutism—meets me in the form of a Jewish returning émigré who came back to Germany in 1945 and collected his revenge.
But why, exactly, is power supposed to be evil in itself?
The power of God is surely good in itself.
Good in itself and in and of itself.
But poor Jacob of Basel experienced the power of human beings, and concluded that power was “evil in itself.”
Let us hope that if power had unfortunately fallen into your own hands, you would not have rejected it—and would therefore have considered power at least capable of being good.
But what about power when it falls into the hands of a human being like this?

If it falls into the hands of a Swiss man, then naturally it is neutral—which means indirect. And if it falls into the hands of a Morgenthau Jew in 1948, then God have mercy on us. Then it appears as the power of the bailiff who flays me with a clear conscience while his employer collects Nobel Peace Prizes.
And now, finally, comes the great front.
Now come all the Antis, the people who reject the friend-enemy distinction as fascist.
The anti-fascists, the anti-alcohol campaigners, the antisemites, against the wine drinkers, against those who defend their homeland, against those who did not emigrate.
The Song of the Totally, Totally Poor German:
I am not an émigré, I was not in the Resistance, I no longer have a chance, I’ll join the Foreign Legion.
(To Friedhelm Kemp, on the occasion of Simone Weil:) How much sadness nests inside the Christian first names of the unbaptized!
